maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OF ITALIAN CONSUL GENERAL
speechtext:
I have risen twice in attempts to answer the question but on both occasions other hon. members have spoken ahead of me.
The hon. member for East Hamilton inquired on Thursday regarding a report in the Ottawa Citizen of February 25 of an address given at a dinner in Ottawa on February 23, by the Consul General of Italy. I had the matter brought to Mr. Petrucci's attention. The following letter has been received from him, dated March 2, 1935:
Consolato Generate TJi S.M.IL Re D'ltalia A1 Canada
Ottawa, March 2, 1935.
Dear Sir:
I note the inquiry in the House of Commons to which you have called my attention.
I regret that the report of my address has given rise to misunderstanding of the purpose and meaning of my remarks. Nothing was further from my mind than to suggest that Italian citizens of Canada should urge "The abandonment of Canada's democratic form of government." I explicitly declared that I did not favour any propaganda. My address gave an analysis of the corporate state, and was mainly concerned with the new economic policies which were being worked out in Italy. I added' that I found that much misunderstanding prevailed on these points, and suggested to my hearers that they might well endeavour to explain the real meaning of the new and interesting experiments that are being made, and which may have something of interest to any people in the present unsettled state of social organization. This suggestion was prompted by a friendly desire to make my country and its recent progress better known to Canadians, and to contribute in this way to still closer understanding between our countries. I added' that the Italian men and women around me were indebted to Canada for their prosperity and expressed the hope that they would always do honour alike to Italy, the country of their origin, and to Canada, the country of their adoption.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
L. Petrucci,
Italian Consul General.
This letter is addressed to O. D. Skelton, Ph.D., M.A., Under Secretary of State for
External Affairs. I am satisfied upon inquiry that the Consul General had no intention of interfering in Canadian affairs. It is only fair that allowance should be made for the difficulty which besets new comers in dealing with the finer points of English speech. I can assure the member for East Hamilton that the government of Canada would not countenance any intervention by a representative of a foreign government in Canadian affairs, or any support from outside to movements for social or economic change in this country. We have our own problems to solve and are entirely capable of solving them by the tried and tested democratic methods which are our heritage.

I find the attitude of some
Liberal members from the province of Quebec very strange, and since- I represent a district in that province I think I should say a few words in answer to what was said last week, particularly by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) and the hon. member for La-prairie-Napierville- (Mr. Dupuis).
The purpose- of this law is to help the farmer who is in financial difficulties. Is there anything wronlg in that? The purpose of this law is to help the farmer who cannot meet his obligations. We have created a system by which the farmer who is in debt goes to his creditors in order to discuss a settlement, to find a remedy to enable him to meet his debts, to adjust his situation, to turn over a new leaf, to start life ane-w, to keep his farm which is the patrimony of his family, and everything that is dear to him. I think some illustrations of what has taken place in the province of Quebec under this legislation will be of greater benefit than any theoretical analysis of the measure itself. I have before me a report in regard to the working of this legislation in the province of Quebec, which states that up to the end of January 9,290 farmers had interviewed receivers. 1,703 proposals had been filed and 226 settlements had been reported as having been voluntarily arrived at before the receivers as between the farmer debtors and their creditors. Over 600 cases had been brought to the attention of the board of review, and up to Saturday, February 16, the board had dealt with 65 cases. It had been successful in most cases in so conciliating the farmers and their creditors that arrangements have been made which were satisfactory to both parties. Further information is to the effect that to the first of this month the board have dealt with 100 cases, instead of 65. The net result in respect of the 65 cases I have mentioned has been a reduction in capital debt of about S100.000 and there also has been a substantial reduction in- the carrying charges, which means that the cost of production will be decreased to that extent.
In order to answer the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville and the hon. member

for Megantic, who spoke of the plight of the farmers of Quebec, and in order to indicate the cooperation that is being developed as between debtors and creditors I should like to refer to one case that was heard by the board of review in Hull, Quebec. The farmer had requested a reduction in his interest rate from six per cent to five per cent, as well as an extension of his mortgage indebtedness. When the creditor who held the hypotheque came before the board of review he consented to the extension and at the same time went further than the farmer had requested by reducing, on his own initiative, the interest rate from six per cent to three per cent.
The board of review is definitely proceeding on the assumption that the principles of conciliation should be applied and that while every reasonable consideration must be given the claims of creditors, at the same time it is absolutely essential to restore the credit of the farmers. Consequently it is in the interests of all concerned that the indebtedness be so rearranged as to insure that the farmer again will be a good credit risk. to say, Mr. Chairman, that the first case is from the judicial district of Beauce. A farmer had a mortgage on his land, and the creditor intended to have the land sold by the sheriff, which would have meant that the farmer would have been left entirely destitute. A meeting of creditors was called, and the creditor compromised the amount of the mortgage, reducing his claim by $500 and reducing the interest rate as well. To indicate how good feeling had been restored between the two, may I say that the creditor, wdiose original intention had been to have the land sold through the sheriff, had come
to the meeting by rail while the farmer had come in his rig, but after the meeting was over, the two returned home in the farmer's rig the very best of friends and with the best of understandings between them.
Case No. 2 comes from the judicial district of Bedford. A farmer had a mortgage debt of $6,500 and ordinary debts amounting to $2,475. In addition to his ordinary debts he had endorsed notes for his son to the amount of $2,600. The farmer asked for a reduction in the mortgage, and in the interest rate, and also asked for a reduction in the ordinary claims. A meeting was held and the creditors could not agree, but later realizing that if the farmer was not- assisted he would not be able to pay the ordinary creditors and that they would lose everything, a second meeting was called and the mortgages were extended, the interest rate was reduced from six to four per cent, and the ordinary creditors agreed to accept 25 per cent of their total claims, $5,075, payable in five yearly payments without interest. All were satisfied with the arrangement.
Case No. 3 came from the judicial district of St. Hyacinthe. A farmer had taken over his father's obligations as the latter was growing old. He faced liabilities of $7,000 besides a very heavy mortgage. He applied to the official receiver and made a proposal to his creditors. The creditors, numbering about twelve, who did not know one another, met and were at first very ill disposed, but the true situation of the farmer was put before them, and after discussing it fully, an arrangement was made with which everybody appeared pleased. The arrangement was ratified by the court. The debtor obtained a reduction of $5,000 in his total liabilities. If he had been sold out by the sheriff the creditors would have received very little, if anything. The official receiver stresses the tolerance of the creditors towards the debtors which is developing as a result of this legislation.

I thought it would be practically impossible for me to bring about any kind of arrangement between this farmer and his creditors. We have heard members on both sides of the house asking for a reduction in interest. This legislation will enable the farmer to apply to the receiver or to the board of review and secure reduction in his interest charges.
On Friday we heard the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville say that the farmers were sorry that they were required to humiliate themselves, as they must do, to take advantage of this legislation. Well, the point I want to make is this, that there is absolutely nothing compulsory in this legislation. This is a mechanism created for the benefit of the farmer. If he wishes to use it in order to reduce his liability he is at liberty to do so, and if he does not wish to avail himself of it, he is equally the master of his own actions.
Then I heard, also on Friday last, the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville qualify this legislation as socialism. As was pointed out by the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville seems to confuse socialism and social legislation. This is the kind of social legislation that we have inaugurated in order to relieve distress and to take care of the farmer and of the working man, and the appellation or qualification of socialism does not disturb us. This is good legislation based on what has been called by high authority social justice-based on the principle of a more just and equitable distribution of wealth. What has been said of the working man is that he must have sufficient wages to supply his family with their ordinary needs: he must have an ample sufficiency for his living. The same must apply to the farmer; he must be enabled to bear the family's burden with greater ease and security, being freed from that hand to mouth uncertainty which is the lot of some of the farmers and working men.

Mr. Chairman, the board of review for the province of Alberta had several sittings in the city of Lethbridge before we left to come to Ottawa, and we had the opportunity of attending and listening to the proceedings. I fancy one would be struck first of all by the informal nature of the hearings. There we found an atmosphere of cooperation and conciliation. The atmosphere of the court was lacking, neither was there any feeling of opposition or antagonism. The members of the board listened very attentively and gave precedence to the representative of the farmers. This gentleman, Mr. McLeod, made it his business, wherever possible, to secure from the farmer
whose case was before the board, just what amount of machinery he had at his disposal, and also tried to form an estimate of his ability to carry on his farming operations. I think the gentleman representing the creditors, Mr. McQuaig, and the representative of the farmers, Mr. McLeod, are sitting on the board of review of our province not as the representatives of one class or another but as men imbued with the one aim, which is to help the farmer get out from under his heavy load of debt and see daylight ahead.
It has been suggested bv several members that we should have a lawyer to present the claims of the farmers to the board. To that suggestion I am opposed. It would bring into that informal hearing the atmosphere of a court, which is not objectionable in any way but whiclf is not the atmosphere in which this act will work to the best advantage. It would mean also a great deal of delay, for the lawyer would endeavour to put forward the best possible case on behalf of his client, and cases which now may be settled in one hour would take at least one day. So I do not think it would be in the interests of the legislation to agree to this suggestion. There appears, however, to be a lack of cooperation between the farm loan board and those in charge of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. We find that several farmers in our neighbourhood have the opportunity of compromising with their creditors, but they are unable to secure any advances, because in our part of the country the banks are not lending money. Both these acts come1 under the Department of Finance, and I am almost persuaded that it might be in the interests of the farmers of western Canada if we had one head administering both acts. I might say also that in Alberta we have had several farmers who have made unjust claims. Some of these men have not been playing the game, and they have been very effectively told by the chairman of the board that their cases were rejected. It has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard that this is not desirable legislation-
I do not like to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I did not make that statement in connection with this legislation. I was referring to the farm loan bill.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that this act was undesirable also, but I accept his correction. So far as the people of my riding are concerned, and I think I can speak for the people of southern Alberta, I believe this is most necessary legislation. When I was

I might also say to him that many reasons can be given because of which this unfortunate depression situation has developed, and one is the lack of policy on the part of the Liberal government from 1921 to 1930. If ever a government lost the market for our agricultural products it was the government of hon. members opposite which held office from 1921 to 1930. To the extent of at least 60,000,000 bushels of wheat per year we lost the European wheat market. Between 1921 and 1930 there was an increase of 39,000,000 acres in the acreage of wheat sown in Europe. I will speak to the committee just as frankly as it appears to my own mind. I had this feeling. In the board of review you have a judge of a superior court as chairman; then you have a prominent barrister who as a matter of fact in every province, so far as I am a ware, commands the respect not only of the bar but of the public as well. It is true that numbers of the loan companies have been represented by counsel, but this is what happens in practice, and what I rather felt at the time would happen. You find the farmer before the board of review, and you find a lawyer representing the creditor. The chairman, the creditor's representative, and also 'the registrar, are men trained in the law, and instinctively all of them prepared to advise and to protect the farmer. But when I made the reply to my hon. friend-it was the reply which I made to the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan branch-I did it in good faith. If experience should indicate that it would be to the advantage of the farmers that counsel should be engaged, they would be, and I may say now that they will be. I may not have put my question correctly, or the minister may have misunderstood me. On the front page of the United Farmer of February 15 last I find a report of a session of the legislature of Alberta in which the following appears;

Could the minister tell the committee whether any communications have been had with the provincial governments in western Canada in regard to including the arrears on school lands in the class of debts which may be dealt with by the board of review? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the question of school lands may have been discussed. The Department of Justice is at present dealing 
with the question whether it would be competent for the provinces to pass legislation to consent to a reduction in the amounts due on school lands. I will have a more succinct answer before the bill leaves this house, but may I point out, notwithstanding that, that it still is competent for the board of review to make findings in reference to and dealing with school lands, as with respect to all other crown lands. As I understand it is only that one point that is being dealt with, whether it is competent for the provinces to consent to a reduction as far as school lands are concerned.

I understood from a member of one of the western boards of review that they understand they have no power to deal with arrears owing on school lands. In discussing that with some of the ministers of western provinces they seemed to think it would be necessary for the dominion government to pass certain legislation, because under the agreement by which the natural resources were turned over to the western provinces they were bound to carry 6ut certain trusts and felt that as long as they were bound by that legislation it would be necessary for the dominion government to pass amending legislation to give them power to allow any compromise to be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be so as far as the point concerning the competency of the provinces is concerned, but it has no bearing on the general statement that the crown is bound by a decision of the board of review, and that its findings would cover school lands as well as others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As far as I am aware no limitation is imposed upon the authority of the board of review to make findings affecting lands, whether of the crown or of companies or private individuals. That holds whether the lands are held by the crown in the right of the province, or in the right of the dominion; and I think without question it includes the lands mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

As the committee is aware

But after the proposal has been filed with the official receiver and prior to the time it is confirmed and filed with the courts, when it is binding, that is the interim of which I was speaking. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The provincial law would
remain in abeyance from the time the proposal was filed. Of course, in the event of the ninety days herein provided expiring, and no new period arising, then he would come under the operation of the provincial debt adjustment act.

That was my point,
namely that in provinces where there is provincial protection a man is not protected either under the provision for sixty days or ninety days on the one hand or by the provincial legislation on the other until such time as the proposal has not only been filed but finally confirmed and filed in the courts.

In that way he loses the protection of the present bankruptcy law and the debt adjustment acts of the respective provinces. It would be well to have that point clear.

I have a

It was intimated that at little or no cost to himself be rcu.'d become a

bankrupt and avoid the difficult situation of having his creditors pursue him all his life. If I am wrong about it I should like to have my impression corrected. If a farmer can refuse to accept an adjustment made by the board, then it is news to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The impression held by
the hon. member for West Edmonton is quite correct up to this point, that if the farmer fails to live up to the terms of the finding, then he does go into bankruptcy. That is quite true.
Irrespective of whether he accepted it or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, quite so. The finding of the board must be binding upon both parties. The provision in this respect is to be found at subsection 3 of section 3 of the original act passed last year:
In any ease where the affairs of a farmer have been arranged by a proposal approved by the court or confirmed by the board as hereinafter provided, part I of the Bankruptcy Act shall notwithstanding section 7 thereof thereafter apply to such farmer but only failure on the part of such farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It continues:
Provided that such failure shall not be deemed an act of bankruptcy if, in the opinion of the court, such act was due to causes beyond the control of such farmer.

But we
have to go back a stage farther than that to find out just how the matter works out. We will suppose Tom Jones goes to a receiver at Calgary and makes a written proposal offering to compromise on his obligations. In such event the secured and probably the unsecured creditors would be consulted. They may disagree with the proposal offered by the farmer and say that they will not accept it. Thereupon the farmer may say, "well, that is my rock bottom proposition; I cannot do any better than that because it represents the limit of my capacity to pay, and I certainly will not enter into any other agreement." Under this act, once a farmer has made a written proposal any secured creditor may pursue the matter through to the board of review and secure a finding by that board which would have the effect of forcing the farmer into bankruptcy, in the event of his not accepting the finding. Let us have the matter clear.
That is my understanding of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right; he stated the situation accurately.

The difficulty is that there may be so many cases waiting for a hearing by a board of review that a case to be heard by it may have to wait ninety days before a decision could be rendered. If the official receiver neglected to ask the court for a stay of proceedings, although a man had done everything he could legally do to have his case heard, and although it may be held up only because of a long list of cases awaiting the action of the board of review, he would be helpless to protect himself against any creditor who might desire to take action against him. I mean by that that he is left in the hands of the receiver, absolutely. I was told by one of the members of the board of review in Alberta that on some days they can hear only three cases, although they put in long hours. Some cases have required that much consideration, if the board wished to be fair to both debtor and creditor. No good purpose would be served in going ahead with this legislation unless the board of review had plenty of time to see that decisions were carefully made. If they are going to give the same consideration to these cases that an ordinary court would give, in many instances they will not be in a position to deal with more than three or four in a day. This afternoon I asked the minister if he could tell how many cases were awainting the decisions of the board of review, and I dare say he may not be in a position to give accurate information on that point. It does seem to me however that according to the figures he gave this afternoon there must be a good many cases in Alberta and' Saskatchewan. I doubt whether in some of the western provinces the board of review would be able to hear in less than ninety days some of the cases which have lately come before them. Therefore I raise the point whether or not ninety days is a long enough period for a stay of proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On March 1, 276 cases had been referred to the board of review in Alberta, and on that date 102 had been heard. While in the earlier stages it is true that only three cases could be heard by the board of review in one day, they have more recently been able to speed up their work. That has been brought about through the experience they have gained and because they are sitting longer hours. They have heard as many as ten cases in a day, so that the hon. member will readily appreciate that the arrearages could very easily be overtaken in a period of time shorter than three months. He speaks about the possible negligence of a registrar in arranging for aD
Farmers' Creditors Act

extension of a stay of proceedings. I think we must assume that the registrar will not be negligent in his duties. While in some cases renewals may be necessary, on the other hand I have had a great many objections from creditors who say they believe the period of three months for a stay of proceedings is too long. On balance therefore, I am inclined to think we have perhaps gone as far as we should, bearing in mind always that the bona fide debtor will not be prejudiced by reason- of the fact that this period can be renewed. On the other hand we must be fair to the creditors and not put them to the unnecessary expense of having to go to court where proceedings are taken under this act only for the purpose of delaying the creditor in the application of his remedy where the proposals are such as could not ultimately be entertained by the board. It seems to me that on balance, three months is a reasonable period.

That was my reason for asking the question. Where a proposal is made and the ninety days expires before further action is taken, and for some reason the application for extension of time is not properly registered and has lapsed, at the expiration of that time would the provincial legislation have full force and afford such protection as would have been afforded had the proposal been before the board? I think it should. The man in such a case is not under the protection of the federal law, and [ should imagine he ought to remain under the protection of the provincial law until such time as the full process has been completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mv hon. friend is quite correct. But even assuming he did not have the right to resort for his protection to the provincial debt adjustment act, in the case instanced by my hon. friend from Macleod it would still be quite competent for him to go before the court and ask for a stay of proceedings, notwithstanding the fact that the steps to do so had not been taken prior to the expiry of the three months period.

It does seem to me that only in a very few cases would a decision be given by tire board of review within ninety days after the farmer had made his proposal. It takes some time after the proposal is first made for the official receiver to notify the creditors and get them to a meeting and get the debtor there, and sometimes they adjourn for a second meeting. The board of review have so many cases on their waiting list that I doubt whether many of them are disposed of within ninety days. If the minister assures us that there is protection through

the official receiver applying to the court for an extension, or through provincial legislation, I certainly do not want to labour the point. But I do submit that not many cases passed on by the board of review will be wound up within ninety days of the first proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend need have no anxiety, certainly so far as Alberta is concerned, because we will assume that the three months has elapsed and that no proceeding has been taken. The creditor before he can sue has to go before the provincial debt adjustment board for a permit before he can proceed at all.
That was my question. Must he? And I understood the minister to say he must.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Furthermore they have a list of all the proposals filed before the official receivers under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.

I do not understand that last statement of the minister. Do I understand that in the event of a decision from the board of review pending and not yet delivered, and the ninety days granted for stay of proceedings having elapsed, the operation of the provincial debt adjustment board will act on behalf of that man? I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the ninety days period has expired, then before the creditor can sue in the province of Alberta he must go before the provincial debt adjustment board to get leave to bring action, notwithstanding the fact that there may be a proceeding then pending before the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
But would he not be under the federal act the day after the ninety days had expired? Would not that be the time the federal act would come into force so far as his creditors were concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, so far as his application is concerned, but not so far as a stay of proceedings is concerned, and that is the point we are discussing at the moment. The stay of proceedings operates for only ninety days

My understanding is that the moment the farmer places himself under the operation of this act he at once ceases to be a ward-shall we call it?- under the debt adjustment board of the province, or has exhausted his right to be a ward until the procedure under this act has been pursued to its ultimate conclusion.

Farmers' Creditors Act

That was not my
understanding as I followed the legislation in this house and in the province. My understanding was that part I of the Bankruptcy Act came into force in the case of an individual farmer only after the proposal had been confirmed and filed with the courts. Up to that time he could commit no breach of conditions until the proposal had been filed with the court. Until the proposal had been filed with the court and the operation was complete he would still be exempt under part I of the Bankruptcy Act and therefore would be subject to the court procedure of the province in respect to proceedings by creditors. That was my understanding, and I am glad that in large measure it has been confirmed by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, as one who
in the course of the practice of his profession has had considerable experience with this a-ct in Alberta, may I take this opportunity to confirm the views expressed by the Minister of Finance? He has put it correctly. When the ninety days stay of proceedings under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has lapsed, the debt adjustment board in Alberta still has to issue a permit for proceedings under the provincial act. To my knowledge the representatives of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in Alberta are closely cooperating with the debt adjustment board officials of the province. I know personally of instances where the space of time having elapsed the debt adjustment board officials first got in touch with the official receiver's office, and upon learning that proceedings had not yet been concluded or that a stay of proceedings had not been extended, refused a permit to issue for proceedings against the debtor.

Before this clause carries I should like to say a few words as I did not have the opportunity to speak on the previous clause.
I wish to shed a different light on this measure as well as on the act which is amended by it. I have just found in my letter box a letter from a good farmer in the province of Ontario, in the part adjoining Quebec, who happens to be the creditor of another farmer. He protests strongly against the enlargement of this legislation. As he points out, he has saved a little money by living a frugal life year after year, and he lent a few dollars to some of his neighbours. One of them has spent his money in luxury. He is the proprietor of two automobiles; he has a piano in his house. He refuses to pay his debt, and now he is putting himself under the protection of this legislation. As

my correspondent says, "I have three boys whom I have to keep, while that man who is spending his money foolishly has only one boy. If he secures accommodation under this law he will be able to get along with his boy but I will be ruined and my three boys will be on the dole list. Why? Because I have saved for twenty years and because I have raised my family with economy and honesty."
I draw the attention of the house to the trend of all this legislation. I do not know the conditions in the western provinces. I presume that a large number of farmers there are indebted to lending companies. But with us in Quebec and in the part of Ontario adjoining Quebec, a very large number of creditors w'ho will be ruined by this law are farmers, small retired farmers living in villages, who have put by a few hundred or a few thousand dollars-a few thousand, very rarely -which they have lent to their fellow citizens living in the same parish, in the same village, relying upon the old traditions of honesty. I well remember the time when money was lent not only without mortgage but without note; money was lent from hand to hand and was always paid back, because the law of honesty was there, much stronger and more effective than any law that can be passed here or in any legislature. What is happening with this law?-and the tendency is increasing. The honest farmer who finds himself in difficult circumstances can hardly obtain credit. Money lenders, whether private citizens or lending companies, tell him that they have no more confidence in the farming community. They say, "If we lend you our money what will happen next year or two years hence? You will go bankrupt. We therefore refuse to give you credit." On the other hand the dishonest farmer takes advantage of this situation. I am afraid that at the rate we are going, making this tendency so much easier, we are fostering dishonesty among the farmers. We are ruining the credit of honest farmers; and at the same time we bring ruin to a large number of individuals, and a very useful class in our community, people who have worked steadily for twenty or thirty years, educated their families in the old traditions of thrift and honesty, and who have helped in their little sphere of action some of their neighbours, some of their fellow farmers, by lending them money. We are ruining one class financially and the other morally.
I do not want to add any more at this time. I suppose my protest is perfectly useless, as it was against another piece of legisla-

Farmers' Creditors Act

tion; because on the eve of an election the temptation, I am afraid, is to look for votes, and to look for votes especially among those people who give their votes according to their interest or their dishonesty. But I protest in the name of the old class of honest, thrifty farmers in my province. I admit that a good deal of extravagance has been going on in the last ten or twenty years, even in Quebec; yet Quebec has preserved more of the old domestic virtues of thrift, honesty, and sparing for old age; and now we are helping to destroy that spirit, we are helping to ruin a class of people who are preserving that spirit. I believe it is wrong economically and socially and for my humble part, although my voice may remain unsupported, I protest against this kind of legislation and against enlarging it all the time, making it easier for the dishonest debtor to cheat his honest creditor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

No doubt there have been instances, I know of instances, where dishonest farmers have attempted to defraud their creditors by using the machinery of this act which was intended to be applied

only to the honest, needy, deserving farmer who could benefit by its provisions. But notwithstanding that fact we have to look at the picture in the large and see what the act is designed to do, and my hon. friend will be the first to admit that it is designed to deal with a class of farmers of whom I have spoken; and when my hon. friend speaks of our amendments enlarging the act, it does so to the extent of extending the stay of proceedings to ninety as against sixty days. It is a difference in degree and not in kind. So far as I am concerned, my hon. friend must remember that I have been resisting the appeals of my hon. friend from Macleod to have the period extended. I thank the minister for his explanation, which I will bring to the attention of my correspondent. I hope it will be effective all through. My hon. friend said that we cannot by law make dishonest people honest. That I quite admit. But we can by law induce honest people to become dishonest, and I am afraid we have done it in many respects. I could point to what has been done in connection with many of our so called social laws adopted since the war. There is no doubt about it in connection with many circumstances arising out of the war, with regard to the adjustment of soldier's claims, the enlargement of the soldiers' pensions legislation and the reversal of the most elementary principle of law in regard to evidence, when we have allowed soldiers to make claims on account of illness which, occurring fifteen years after the war, they attribute to the war itself, forcing the government to prove that it did not originate in the war. I remember, in the previous parliament, giving an instance of horrible frauds committed in that way by some returned soldiers. My remarks are general and go beyond the scope of that clause, as I explained, because I was not here when the first clause was discussed. But I thank the minister again for his explanation and I hope the press at least of Quebec will make it quite clear that in such cases as this the attention of the board of review should be directed to the necessity of protecting the honest people,

Before the bill is reported
let me say that I have repeatedly urged upon the house the necessity for providing some general act to limit the rate of interest on farm mortgages. I think hon. members will recall that when this act was being passed a year ago I with many other members urged very strongly on the Prime Minister that it was necessary to give to all farmers some protection in regard to interest rates. This legislation I am sure will not benefit more than ten per cent of the farmers, In other words at least ninety per cent will not take advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Many farmers are still paying interest at the rate of eight and even nine per cent per annum. I still feel very strongly that we should include in this act some provision for reducing rates of interest on all farm mortgages. What I am anxious to do is to prevent a great many farmers who are included in the ninety per cent of which I spoke from being forced into a state of bankruptcy through the payment of too high interest rates. Almost every agricultural country in the world except Canada has passed legislation of this nature, reducing rates of interest on farm debts.	Canada
should not lag behind in this respect. Anyone who has collected interest at the rate of eight or nine per cent during the last five years has had in almost every case purchasing power greatly in excess of the purchasing power of money at the time the loan was made, so that a reduction in the rate of interest during these latter years would not have been a reduction in the purchasing power of these people.
For the purpose of bringing this matter before the committee I wish to move an amendment to the bill. Before doing so I would draw attention to section 17 of the present act which reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other statute or law, whenever any rate of interest exceeding seven per centum is stipulated for in any mortgage of farm real estate, if any person liable to pay the mortgage tenders or pays to the person entitled to receive the money, the amount owing on such mortgage and interest to the time of payment, together with three months' further interest in lieu of notice, no interest shall after the expiry of three months' period aforesaid, be chargeable, payable or recoverable in respect of the said mortgage at any rate in excess of five per centum per annum.
The purpose of that, I think, is clear; that if any mortgagor can get the money and

Farmers' Creditors Act
tender it in payment to the mortgagee, the mortgagee must accept payment of his principal, or thereafter be content with interest at five per cent per annum. It seems to me that there was very good reason for placing the rate at five per cent per annum; the government felt that five per cent was a fair rate under the circumstances. Of course few farmers have been able to secure the full amount of their mortgage to tender payment of the principal sum so as to get the rate of interest reduced to five per cent. I do not think we should be working much hardship on any person; on the other hand it would be in the interest of the great majority, and we should be following much the same line as has been followed in almost every other country in dealing with farm debts, if we passed legislation effecting a reduction in the rate of interest on farm mortgages. In order to bring the matter properly before the committee I move:
That Bill No. 10, an act to amend The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, be amended by adding the following section thereto:-
6.	Section seventeen of the said act is amended by adding the following subsections thereto:-
(3)	No interest at a rate exceeding five per centum per annum shall be charged, payable or recoverable on any existing mortgage of farm real estate, or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate.
And because I believe that this should be retroactive and should cover the past four years of very low prices I have added another subsection:
(4)	Where interest at a rate in excess of five per centum per annum has been paid from and after the first day of January, 1931, on any mortgage or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate, the difference between the rate of five per centum and the amount paid or collected shall be credited on any arrears of interest outstanding, and if there are no arrears, then the difference shall be credited on the principal of the mortgage or agreement.
In support of my amendment asking for a reduction in the rate of interest during the years 1931, 1932 and 1933, may I point out again that the average farm income in Canada, which was approximately $1,600 in 1928 and $1,500 in 1929, fell to $740 in 1931, to $660 in 1932, and in 1933 to $640. Anyone reading these figures will realize that it was much easier for a farmer to pay even ten or twelve per cent in 1928 and 1929 than five per cent in these later years. Because of the very difficult situation in which the farmers have found themselves in the last five years due to the very low prices received
for their products, prices over which they had no control, I ask favourable consideration of this amendment by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was not in the house last year when section 17 was added to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, but it will be apparent to any draftsman that it is a section which has no relation whatsoever to that act. I have no doubt that the reason it was placed there was that it was not thought advisable at that stage of the session to introduce a fresh amendment to the Interest Act. But that is where a section of this kind ought to go. However, section 17 is there.
Now, may I point out that the proposed amendment-of which the hon. member for Macleod was good enough to give a copy in advance, for which I thank him-makes a provision which calls for an expenditure of public money. It is no less public money by reason of the fact that it comes from the farm loan board, for the principal comes out of the public exchequer. Therefore his amendment calling as it does for the expenditure of public money, is out of order, and it would be necessary to raise that point. But may I point out to my hon. friend that at the present moment he has a bill before the banking and commerce committee dealing with the rate of interest, and there is no reason why the whole subject should not be comprehensively dealt with there, so that any action taken by the committee on banking and commerce would be uniform. That would deal with the matter as one of interest and not as one affecting this bill, because I submit that it has no bearing whatever on this bill. The compromise of the debts of a farmer has no relation whatsoever to the question of interest, because it is a matter of compromise. Whether the interest is one per cent or twenty-five per cent would make no difference in the adjustment of the debts. Under the circumstances I hope that my hon. friend will not press his amendment but will take the course I have suggested; otherwise I shall have to raise the point of order which I have mentioned.

Whether rightly or wrongly I am not going to say now, of course, but last year by section 17 of this very act the government itself did bring this question of interest within the scope of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Unfortunately they placed in the act a weapon that was most unworthily used in some cases by unscrupulous persons who alleged, of course, that the government had reduced the interest rate to five per cent. Those who studied the clause realized, of
Farmers' Creditors Act

course, that in itself it was practically useless, and I doubt if a single case has been adjudicated under it. The clause provided, as the hon. member for Macleod has pointed out, that where a debtor farmer tendered the payment of all the principal due, all the arrears due and all the interest due plus three months' interest in advance, after the three months had elapsed no rate of interest higher than five per cent could be collected. When you make a statement of that kind to an average farmer audience in western Canada it is greeted with scornful laughter, and quite properly so. The clause is worthless. I congratulate the hon. member for Macleod on endeavouring to introduce into this act the very principle that the government protested it had in mind last year, the general reduction of interest rates of five per cent, in keeping with the action taken in other countries. It is not my purpose to-night to stress the necessity for that; it has been shown again and again in other years as well as this year.

Would
the hon. gentleman read section 17?

It will be read in a moment. I could tell hon. members of men who came to Canada from other countries; I have one in mind at the moment, who came here with some $35,000. He entered into the purchase of land under an agreement of sale; he operated as a scientific farmer, sparing himself neither in physical toil nor in mental effort. He worked twenty-five years without leaving his farm, but at the end of that time it was found that he owed $63,000, half to the Canadian Pacific Railway and half to the Bank of Montreal. Two years ago his life insurance policy, his last realizable asset, was sold, and the proceeds were divided equally between the bank and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That result, of course, was due in large part to climatic conditions over which neither the debtor nor the creditor had control, but at the same time the ruthlessness of collection by the creditors and the extortionate rate of interest charged in relation to the productivity of the farm had no small bearing on the man's ultimate collapse.
I hold in my hand a statement which I gave the house last year, but which possibly has been forgotten. It is the result of research work carried on by Doctor Win Allen and Doctor Hope of the university of Saskatchewan. After two years of study they found that if the farmers of Saskatchewan had wanted to pay the interest on the farm debt- the interest only-according to their investigation it would have required four-fifths of

the entire wheat crop raised and sold in that province. If they had wanted to pay their taxes-with which we are not concerned at the moment-it would have required two-fifths of the total wheat crop raised and sold. So if the farmers of that province had endeavoured to pay interest and taxes alone it would have required one-fifth more wheat than they raised and sold. Exactly similar conditions prevail, varying only slightly in degree, in the three western provinces where grain is the principal source of revenue.
A few days ago the hon. member for Macleod again	drew vividly	to the	attentionof the house the collapsed financial condition of agriculture. He must have made it apparent to every hon. member who listened to	him that it	is impossible	foragriculture	to continue to pay	even	fiveper cent,	or certainly	more	than	five
per cent. I think he is exceedingly conservative in placing the figure at five per cent; if I had my way I would eliminate all interest from the time this depression commenced, and I would not restore it until we had price levels analogous in some degree with those of 1926. The figures quoted by the hon. member for Macleod are worth putting on Hansard once more. He stated that the total farm income in Canada for the four pre-depression years amounted in round figures to $4,012,000,000. In the four years of the depression that total income was only $1,740,000,000, so there was a decline in income of $2,268,000,000 during that four year period. These figures are significant; they tell a story, more vividly than words, of conditions that must be dealt with by this parliament and that must be recognized by this government. The proposal made by the hon. member for Macleod, even if it were out of order-and I contend it is not-ought to be accepted by the government and introduced as their own measure. If they are not willing to accept it as an amendment from this section of the house let them accept the principle and bring in the amendment themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Bow
River is too shrewd to have misunderstood my position. I am not dealing with the merits of the interest question at all. I have stated time and again that I should like to see interest rates as low as they can be reasonably made, but the question of interest does not arise in connection with this bill at all; it has no reference to it. The hon. member says section 17 was placed in the bill last year by the government. That is quite true. The only explanation I can offer is that at that stage of the session it was thought

Farmers' Creditors Act
perhaps unwise to attempt to amend the Interest Act, but the bill was altogether silent on the question of interest. That would have no bearing upon the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. The settlement is made in the first place by compromise between debtor and creditor, and it does not make any difference whether the rate is ten per cent, seven per cent or two per cent; it is a question of settlement. Then you come to the board of review, who make their own terms with respect to interest. So the question of interest has no bearing on the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act whatever. The government has taken a stand so far as its general policy with respect to interest rates is concerned; we have come to the point where we have received many complaints from savings bank depositors that the rates of interest are too low. That is just an aside. I have told the hon. member for Macleod and I now tell the committee that the question of interest is one that should be dealt with in connection with the Interest Act, and my hon. friend from Macleod now has a bill dealing with the question of interest which is being considered in the banking and commerce committee. I am not trying to evade responsibility, so far as the government are concerned, in dealing with the question of interest on its merits. But having regard to the question of propriety, so far as the committee is concerned there is no question about this amendment being out of order. It is one of the cardinal rules of the house that only at the instance of the crown, by way of message, can a measure be submitted involving the expenditure of public money.
Mr. HA'NBURY: In what way would that involve an expenditure of public money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because the amendment
provides not only that there should be a certain fixed rate of interest, but that where more than five per cent has been paid an amount shall be returned to the borrower.

To the one who holds
the mortgage. It may be a private individual it does not necessarily have to be the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This will affect mortgages made under the farm loan board.

But is it not a general
provision affecting all mortgages, and not necessarily only farm loan mortgages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Even so, it will affect the
farm loan board.

Could the minister explain
how government money is involved in this transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have done so often, and I do not know whether I can do it any clearer. All the money which is lent under the farm loan act comes out of the public exchequer, and if the farm loan board has to hand back four years' interest, that money would have to come out of the public treasury.

I am not quite clear
whether we are now discussing the amendment or the point of order. I shall assume however for a moment that we are discussing the amendment. I understand-and if I have the wrong impression I hope the minister will correct me at once-that the legislation of last year called the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, now being amended, had as its objective not only the protection of farmers against what might be described as unfair foreclosures, but also the possible reduction of farmers' debts. If that was the intention of the act then I believe the minister will have great difficulty in excluding a discussion of interest rates, because the debts of a great many farmers consist almost entirely of interest. More than fifty per cent of most debts of long standing is composed of interest which those farmers have been unable to pay. Therefore if we are effectively to enable the farmers to reduce their debts, the most direct way to do it would be reduce the interest rate, the chief cause of a growing debt which cannot be paid. That fact in itself disposes of the minister's objection to the effect that the proper place for the amendment would be as an amendment to the Interest Act. Since the amendment has for its objective the reductions of farmers' debts I suggest it quite properly comes up for consideration at this time.
Under the act which was passed last year of farmer may offer a mortgage company the complete amount of his mortgage, even though it may not be due, and if the mortgage company does not feel inclined to accept the payment the farmer must from that time forward obtain his loan at the rate of five per cent. That is alll very well, but the principle involved is that a man able to pay on his mortgage can get it at five per cent, whereas the poor devil who can pay nothing must continue to pay seven or eight per cent or, in some cases, ten per cent. Surely there is no common sense in an arrangement like that. Certainly when passing legislation such as that now before us we ought to be fair
Farmers' Creditors Act

enough to arrange it so that the man who has very little will receive favours equal to those received by the man who has more.

The hon. member for Bow
River thinks that when I placed the rate of interest at five per cent I set it too high. I believe I should plead guilty to that charge. I know such a rate would prove to be a heavy burden upon the farmer, but the rate of five per cent is mentioned in section 17 of the act passed last year.

Read
the section.

I read it before, but I shall do so again:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other statute or law whenever any rate of interest exceeding seven per centum is stipulated for in any mortgage of farm real estate, if any person liable to pay the mortgage tenders or pays to the person entitled to receive the money the amount owing on such mortgage and interest to the time of payment, together with three months' further interest in lieu of notice, no interest shall after the expiry of three months' period aforesaid be chargeable, payable or recoverable in respect of the said mortgage at any rate in excess of five per centum per annum.
2. The provisions of this section shall apply in the case of any mortgage heretofore or hereafter made and whether or not the principal sum is due and owing at the time such tender or payment is made.
Who moved that last year?

This is a section of the bill introduced by the government at the last session. When the matter was under discussion last year I believe hon. members will recall that we spent the greater part of a day trying to persuade the Prime Minister to change this section so that the rate of interest on any mortgage should not be more than five per cent per annum from and after the passing of the act. I still feel strongly that that should have been done. I believe, further, that the preamble to the act introduced last year would justify our including some provision for a general cut in the rate of interest on farm mortgages. The act passed last year was to deal with one thing only, namely farm debts. The first half of the preamble reads as follows:
Whereas in view of the depressed state of agriculture the present indebtedness of many farmers is beyond their capacity to pay; and' whereas it is essential in the interest of the dominion to retain the farmers on the land as efficient producers....
It seems to me one of the things we need to-day is a general reduction in interest rates, so that those farmers may be kept on the
IMr. Irvine.]
land as efficient producers. Interest rates of eight and nine per cent will in the course of the next four or five years, if we continue to receive low prices, drive into bankruptcy a number of farmers who are still solvent. Present rates of interest are too high and are more burdensome to the farmers than the amount of the debt. We could reduce the amount of the debts by one-quarter, without touching the rate of interest, and not give the farmer as much relief as we could give by reducing the rate of interest. I do not believe we would be working a great hardship on anybody. We would not be cancelling any savings; we would simply be reducing to five per cent the rate of interest to be collected, and in most cases the five per cent would have as great purchasing power as the eight per cent charged in 1929.
Then the minister raised the further point, namely that in effect the amendment would call for the payment of moneys out of the public funds. Perhaps I am not learned in the law-I will admit that-but it does seem to me that the minister's observations could not apply to the amendment. It simply states:
Where interest at a rate in excess of five per centum per annum has been paid from and after the first day of January, 1931,-
And since that time we have had these extremely low prices-
-on any mortgage or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate, the difference between the rate of five per centum and the amount paid or collected shall be credited on any arrears of interest outstanding, and if there are no arrears then the difference shall be credited on the principal of the mortgage or agreement.
Therefore it would not be necessary to return any money to the mortgagor. The amendment simply means that money which has been paid and credited to interest would in some cases have to be credited as payment on principal. It seems to me that in that case there is no provision calling for an expenditure of public money. I may be wrong, but at any rate that is my present view, and I hope the chairman of the committee will hold a similar one.
Then, in regard to the other point, I admit quite frankly that the matter of interest rates is now before the banking committee in the form of a bill which I introduced, but that deals with interest rates in general. In none of its provisions does it relate specifically to the rate of interest on farm mortgages. It seems to me therefore that this committee would be in order to deal with the rate of interest on farm mortgages, and that we may properly do so when we are considering the

Farmers' Creditors Act
bill having for its purpose the amending of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I trust that upon reflection the minister will see the reasonableness of my suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Macleod seems to think there is a distinction between giving up several hundreds of thousands of dollars of money on the one hand, and paying it on the other. Well, there may be, but I do not see it myself. Here is the effect of this amendment of my hon. friend, in its actual concrete results. I am not stressing the point of order which I think is very clear. The farm loan board of Ontario has out today something like S55,000,000, the Saskatchewan board has out 818,000.000; the Alberta board has out some 812,000,000, and at the present moment the Saskatchewan board is lending money to farmers at six and a half per cent. H my hon. friend's amendment were carried it would mean that the farm loan board of Saskatchewan would have to hand back one and a half per cent of all their mortgage money covering the last five years, and in the last three years alone it would run into many hundreds of thousands of dollars. So it is idle for my hon. friend to say that this would not work a hardship. It certainly would, but I make that observation in reply to the statement of my hon. friend who seems to think that in a matter of dealing with a few hundreds of thousands of dollars or a few millions it would not do any harm at all, that they do not pay it-they just credit it. Yet the fact remains that you are out just that much money, whether you pay it or credit it. I hope the committee in its judgment will be disposed to reject this amendment, if only on the ground of equity and justice. But I submit, Mr. Chairman, that under the rules of the house it is not competent for my hon. friend to move it.
Does the hon. member press his amendment?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I would like to have your ruling whether it is in order or not.

I just want to say one word, Mr. Chairman. I am in absolute sympathy with the amendment moved by the 'hon. member for Macleod, and ordinarily speaking I would support it if it were moved by the government. On the other hand, I must agree with the Minister of Finance that the amendment is out of order as it either inferentially or directly affects the revenues of the crown.
If it is ruled out of order, the fact that it is out of order does not permit the government to escape responsibility.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that the amendment has been found to be out of order, but if I have your permission, sir, I wonder if I might move the first part of it now as an amendment to the bill. It occurs to me that if the second part of the amendment is out of order perhaps the first part is in order. Therefore I would move that section 17 of the act be amended by adding the following subsection thereto:
No interest at a rate exceeding five per centum per annum shall be charged, payable or recoverable on any existing mortgage of farm real estate or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate.
The committee will see that I have left off that section to which objection has been taken on the ground that it would necessitate the expenditure of public money. I still feel that this is a matter which we might very well deal with; as a matter of fact I think we should deal with it now that we are considering the question of farm debts. I therefore move this amendment, Mr. Chairman, and hope that it will be accepted.

I should like to say a word in support of this amendment. I frankly confess that in spite of having full sympathy with the amendment previously proposed by the hon. member for Macleod I kept quiet because even before the Minister of Finance had spoken I was convinced that it was out of order because of its application to loans made by public bodies. But I do not think that objection applies to the amendment that has just been proposed. It might be considered under two aspects, and I shall not dwell upon either.
Supply-M arine

First there is the question of the merits of the case itself; that is, the relation of that reduced interest rate to farm prices and farm income and farm purchasing power. That has been so well argued that I shall not deal with it at all. But may I point out this one fact. Such action would perhaps do more to safeguard the creditors and make many doubtful debts sound and payable than any other action that could be taken. It has been pointed out before that one of the chief factors in increasing the risk in lending money, the risk of non payment, is the fact that in many if not in most cases the rate of interest is higher than can be earned by the money. To reduce that rate to a more reasonable point would go further than almost anything else could go in safeguarding the ultimate rights of the creditor and making possible his ultimate repayment.
The point has been raised, however-the minister has not discussed the merits of the question-as to the relation of this question to the present bill now under discussion. It has been suggested by the minister that this is not the proper place to deal with such a subject, but that it should be dealt with under the general Interest Act. Well, we are ruled largely by precedent in this house, and action taken at one time unchallenged and passing into law becomes a precedent which governs the application of that principle for the future. To my mind when the government last year introduced the principle of interest regulation in relation to this act, it was not done by accident; it was not done haphazard; it was not merely attached without any possible correlation; it formed a very definite part of the whole plan. It seems to me that such an amendment could find no better place than in an act the purpose of which is to reduce debt and to reduce interest and to bring debt and interest within the payable range of the farmer. I shall not stress that point, which is appreciated I am sure by every hon. member. I only hope the government will look favourably upon this amendment. Lacking the assurances that general and drastic action will be taken in respect of the Interest Act itself, I do hope that the government and this committee will consider favourably the application of this principle to the particular type of debt with which we are dealing under this act, mortgage debts owed by farmers.

Again
on a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I understand that the Chair ruled that the entire amendment moved by the hon. member for

Macleod was out of order. As such, both subsections 3 and 4 fall by the same ruling of the Chair. Do I understand that any hon. member has moved a new amendment? If no new amendment has been moved, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that your ruling places out of order all the subsections of the previous amendment. On the other hand, if a new amendment has been submitted to the Chair I would with respect submit that subsection 3 by itself is in order, reading:
No interest at a rate exceeding five per centum per annum shall be charged, payable or recoverable on any existing mortgage of farm real estate or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate.
I do not think that that does directly, although it might inferentially, affect the revenues of the crown in the years to come. But I submit that unless some other member has moved a new amendment, the entire amendment that was originally moved by the hon. member for Macleod has fallen by the ruling of the Chair.
