I wish to bring to the attention of the minister certain things that are happening in connection with the unemployment camps under the jurisdiction of vhe Department of National Defence. Last year when this subject was under discussion I called the attention of the then minister to certain matters in connection with supplies to the camps in British Columbia, and to-night I want to refer particularly to the two in my constituency at White Rock. Last year I made an appeal with regard to the purchasing of supplies for these camps, pointing out that when the camps were under the jurisdiction of the provincial government that government had a policy of purchasing supplies from farmers round about. They would purchase fresh milk, fresh vegetables, potatoes, beef, pork, and so forth, paying the prevailing
wholesale prices. After the camps came under the jurisdiction of the dominion government that policy was changed and the supplies were purchaser by tender or contract from wholesale firms in Vancouver. I pointed out last year that an injustice was being done the farmers in that the government was paying three or four prices for the goods they were purchasing from the wholesalers, and the then minister informed me that if the farmers would club together or if an organization of them would submit prices to the government they would be taken into consideration, but that under the circumstances it was deemed in the best interests to purchase supplies for the camps from wholesalers. I pointed out, however, that it was difficult to carry this out. This year I made it my business to pay a visit to those camps. Last year I had paid one or two visits to them, but just prior to leaving for Ottawa I paid another to see what was being done in the matter of supplies. One of the first things I examined there was potatoes and other vegetables. I have brought along with me to show the committee a sample of the potatoes they had in those camps, and am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not in his seat because I think the exhibit of potatoes I have on my desk is well worthy of his investigation. The farmers in the fall of last year were unable to sell their potatoes in any quantity. First-class grade 1 potatoes, were being sold for $5 a ton landed in the city of Vancouver. As for second grade potatoes, there was practically no sale for them, but if any were sold, the most any farmer received was $3.75 a ton. I was very much surprised when I visited the camp to find out that the government was purchasing potatoes from a firm by the name of F. R. Stewart. I may say to the committee that is one firm which should be investigated, because it is part and parcel, I believe, of a United States combine that is operating on the Pacific coast and squeezing out the lifeblood of the farmer. I was greatly surprised to find that the government was paying $24 a ton for potatoes a sample of which I now hold in my hand and which I am going to send across to the minister, because such stuff at the price is a positive disgrace. I took from the camp a sample, namely, these three potatoes which I am now passing across the floor; I took them into Vancouver and placed them before one of the dominion government inspectors. He, believing that I had a few tons to sell, said, "Mr. Reid, those potatoes are not worth much; you could not sell them at this time." I replied, "Supposing I were selling them and someone wanted to
Supply-National Defence

buy them; what would they pay me?" He said, "You would probably get $3.50 or $3.75 a ton landed in Vancouver." I said that I was much obliged for the information. The potatoes were grade 2, or perhaps grade 3, and that is what the dominion government is paying $24 a ton for. One farmer who lived in the vicinity, on hearing that the camp was out of potatoes, went to the camp foreman and asked if he could deliver a few tons. The foreman said, "Well I am very sorry, but you will have to take the matter up with the purchasing agent." The purchasing agent in turn said, "Well, F. R. Stewart is supplying the camp with potatoes." So this farmer telephoned Mr. F. R. Stewart, who said to him, "Well, do not send the potatoes to the camp; bring them in here and if we can take them we will take them from you." Mr. Stewart took a few tons for which I believe he paid the farmer $5 a ton landed in Vancouver, and this firm in turn took the potatoes out to the same district and charged the government $24 a ton for them. I think I am right in drawing this matter to the attention of the committee. Last year also I drew to the attention of the committee and the former minister what was happening in regard to the purchase of supplies.
A similar situation prevails with regard to milk. They are purchasing tinned milk when they are right in a district where fresh milk is easily procurable. I understand they are paying about $12 a ton for vegetables when all the farmer was getting was about $4 a ton for carrots, $6 a ton for turnips and about $9 a. ton for cabbage, which is the highest priced vegetable there. But these vegetables are all taken out of the district where the camp is, trucked eighteen to twenty miles into Vancouver, and then taken right out again to the camp. I would not feel so strongly about this were it not for the fact that I had already appealed to the government in regard to this sort of thing. It is high time that we had a number of hanging posts throughout the country, because any man who takes advantage of the people when such suffering is going on should be drastically dealt with. I can now understand the feeling that prevailed in days gone by when they hanged the sheep stealers.
I also complained last year, not publicly in the house but otherwise, regarding a firm that got a contract for supplying tobacco to the camp. The men there by the way are receiving between $5 and $6 a month and all their clothing, and I think I am correct in saying that they are allowed one and one-quarter cents a day for tobacco. The firm

that got the contract for tobacco last year got it I believe at a price of forty-five cents a pound, and the local firm in my city complained to me that the Imperial Tobacco Company had undercut everyone else and obtained the contract at a price away below cost of production. The men in the camp receive one and one-quarter cents, so they got one and one-quarter cents worth of tobacco a day, and the price then was forty-five cents a pound. But I was greatly surprised when I visited the camp to find out that by some juggling the price had been jacked up quite a bit without any of the other firms being given a chance to bid again. The result was that the men in the camp were of course getting less tobacco than before. It is high time that a thorough investigation was made into the matter of purchasing supplies in those camps.
It was stated in the provincial house-I have not the exact facts before me, but I have the information on the authority of engineers who have looked into the matter- that the purchase of all clothing and the total overhead expenditure coupled with the 5 to 6 dollars a month given to the men is costing the government in the neighbourhood of from $30 to $40 a month to maintain each single man in those camps. That statement was made in all seriousness in the provincial house by those who have investigated the matter, although the figure they gave was a little higher than the one I am now submitting. I got this figure independently before I came to Ottawa. When one looks over the long list of stuff which is supplied to these men and realizes the nature of the firms that are supplying it, if they are supplying it along the same line as that firm is doing with regard to potatoes, I can well understand that the cost to the country would be high to maintain those single men in the unemployment camps. Those matters are very serious and, as I say, this is not the first time I have drawn them to the attention of the Minister of National Defence.
I am not at all sure whether the single unemployed transient comes under the minister's department or under the Minister of Labour, but I might as well complete the story that I have, because this is affecting all the municipalities and cities in British Columbia; and the situation is becoming very much worse due to the actions of and a ruling that was made under the Department of National Defence. Rules were made regarding transient men, but a new rule was issued last fall I understand whereby men must be physically one hundred per cent

Supply-National Defence
perfect before they are taken into the camps. I have the case of two brothers who came I believe from Alberta; they were transients of course coming from one province to the other and were looking for work. When they arrived in Vancouver they were told that the first thing they would have to do would be to go before a doctor to be tested before they went to those camps. The two of them went before a doctor. One of them was pronounced one hundred per cent perfect, but the doctor said that the other had certain imperfections in his teeth and he was denied access to the unemployment camp. The relief officers who have been handling the affairs for the cities and municipalities complain very bitterly about the number of men who are coming from other provinces and who must first undergo a medical examination before being accepted in the camp. It seems strange the men must be one hundred per cent or thereabouts before being accepted in these [DOT]camps, and that those who are not are simply thrown on the street. Were it not for social organizations and the charity of the cities and of the provincial government, it is hard to say just what might happen to those single transients who are moving from one province to another. This movement has been the cause of a great burden on the various cities and the government of British Columbia. They have come into that province by the thousands. I was at the boundary last fall when a Ford car with a family of eleven in it was on its way to British Columbia, and these people were not there long until they were on relief. The youngest of that family was aged nine. I have seen many schoolboys piled into a car but I never knew of as many in a Ford as on that occasion. Then we have people having their fares paid to British Columbia; I think that practice should be brought to the attention of the government. Many of these people have come into the province and some have been placed in the camps. I have under my hand an affidavit as to the fares of two being paid by the city of Winnipeg to British Columbia. That is one of the most despicable practices that is going on at this time; they are just trafficking in human life. If they find that people have a notion of going somewhere they say, "We will gladly pay your fare." I do not know how many have been sent east, but my guess is that the majority have gone west on account of our more equable climate. We knew this practice was being carried on by many cities, but this was the first person
we had who would make an affidavit. The others were rather scared, but this one in Surrey made affidavit that the city of Winnipeg gave them their fare to British Columbia. They soon become a charge on the municipality. I think these matters should be brought to the attention of the government. But I want to stress particularly these matters which come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defence, with regard to supplies and tobacco and the inspection of the men before they are taken into the camps. I brought this up last year but was told: "Oh well, we would rather deal with a firm that can supply us for two or three months than with individual farmers." It is no wonder the men in those camps are discontented and have lost heart, because every man there knew that the government was paying $24 a ton for potatoes when farmers in the district could not sell them. They knew that the government was paying a high price to the wholesaler for vegetables and other supplies, and I suppose they must have said to themselves: What is the use of our doing anything when the government allows this graft to go on? I appeal to the minister to have this practice stopped, and go back to the former method of purchasing fresh milk and other supplies from the farmers and give them some benefit. I did not hear many complaints when the provincial government was purchasing supplies direct from the farmers. It seems idiotic to have them trucked in to the wholesaler at Vancouver and then for that wholesaler to truck them back at a price that I say should not be allowed him.

I also have a little story to tell in regard to the relief camps in my riding. I have wondered many times how long the present system will be carried on. I have made the statement in British Columbia and this house, and I am going to make it again, that the way those camps are conducted is a disgrace to the people of Canada and an insult to the majority of the boys housed in them. They would not be there if they could get a job; it is not that they are looking for something easy. After last session I made investigations-not by sitting in my office in an arm chair; I visited the camps and talked to the boys. Plenty of them are ablebodied fellows; all they needed was a square deal to get some results. On July 25 last I wrote to the then Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland). I would like to place on Hansard my letter and the minister's reply:
Supply-National Defence

Dear Mr. Sutherland:
In my federal riding of Vancouver North you have three relief camps under your department. One is located at Squamish, one located at Halfmoon bay and the other at Pender harbour.
These camps are favourably located for having some really worth while work done on the roads, but under the present system of 201 cents per day, they will never finish the job they are working at.
The road from Squamish to Britannia, about seven miles, would' be wonderful value to the Squamish valley, where there are a lot of settlers and they have no market except by railway or steamship. If this piece of road from Squamish to Britannia was finished, it would give the farmers and settlers in the Squamish valley access to the mine at Britannia, where they have a mine in operation employing on the average 1,000 men, and all their supplies shipped in by water. So I think you can see at a glance it would be a job worth while if this road could be finished. May say that Britannia mines have ore in sight for many years. This alone would justify the building of the road.
There is a highway from Gibsons landing, to Pender harbour all completed except about two miles, which is located between the Pender harbour camp and the Halfmoon bay camp. If this were completed it would be of wonderful service to the travelling public.
The present system to me is an insult to humanity. I visited the camps and there are plenty of able-bodied men who would be able to build these two connecting links and open up these roads in a short time, provided they were given a reasonable deal.
My suggestion would be that you make an exception of these three camps and pay the minimum wage, which would be 40 cents per hour, work them say five hours a day, and five days per week, charge them &0 cents per day for board and let them pay for their own clothing.
I can assure you if this were put into effect there would be a different atmosphere, everybody would be satisfied, and you would create some work which would be of lasting benefit.
Might say they have accommodation at Squamish for about 130 men. The other two camps can handle fifty or sixty men, which would be enough for their smaller job.
I have been in the construction business all my life and I know whereof I speak, and if you could adopt the suggestion as outlined, you would get results and there would be three relief camps in British Columbia being paid a reasonable wage and I will guarantee you will get good results.
I hope you will give this your prompt and careful attention.
The minister replied on July 31, saying: Dear Mr. Munn,-
I thank you for your letter of July 25 regarding the camps which our department is maintaining in your riding.
It -would be impossible to have one system of organization in connection with certain camps and not in others. I realize fully the difficulties existing at the present time. Please be assured that your letter will be given every consideration.

I have had no further word, and the camps are still there. In those three camps to-day I think there are between three and four hundred men. They have caused a good deal of trouble, and it is not surprising that there should be dissatisfaction: they get twenty cents a day and indifferent board, and the hon. member for New Westminster has told about the tobacco and other luxuries that they have to buy with that twenty cents a day. I protest very emphatically against that system. The government should change it and there should be a clean-up in those relief camps without any further delay. It is a disgrace to the people of British Columbia and of Canada and an insult to the boys housed in them.

I wish to add a little to what has been said by the two hon. members who have preceded me. Living as I do in the city of Vancouver I have been in touch with men from the unemployment camps during the last two or three years. Instead of conditions in the camps improving, as they should if the department administering them would benefit by experience, they are getting worse and worse. About the Christmas season of last year some seven or eight hundred of the men left the camps and came to Vancouver. In one instance at least their transportation from the camp to the city was paid; the -men from the other camps came on their own. This became quite a problem in the city of Vancouver; they had their own relief troubles and could not -offer to look after this additional burden. However, they could not very well turn down the men because to do so without having some agency to provide for them would be rather a serious thing for the city. Some members of the council of social agencies took up the case on behalf of the -men and arranged for meals and beds for a few days, until such time as they could get in touch with the provincial government and have them approach the federal government in the matter. I was advised of the situation very early in the proceedings, and with several others I interested myself on behalf of the men. We found it very difficult to get anything done. However, after coming here to Ottawa we found why that was so: the reason was that the attorney general of British Columbia had been advised by the Prime Minister of Canada that no provision whatever should be made for the men but that they should be forced through starvation to go back to the camps, regardless of what the conditions in the camps were.

Supply-National Defence
One of the things for which the men were asking was an investigation into camp conditions. It seems to me that even though these men are on relief they should not lose all their rights of citizenship. They are on reilef through no fault of their own; it is the fault of society, and that being the case I believe when they make repeated complaints those complaints should be investigated. We took the matter up with the city council of Vancouver; we took with us a delegation of the men to state their own case to the civic authorities. The men did not say conditions were bad in all camps; at least they said some camps were worse than others. I was going to say some were better than others, but I think I should put it the other way about. I am not saying whether or not this is true, but true or not I think it is sufficient basis for an investigation. One of the men told us that in his camp conditions were fairly good. They had a good cook, who was feeding them fairly well. But after some little time the superintendent came around and told the cook that he was exceeding the per capita allowance, and that the food would have to be cut down. Evidently the cook was a fairly decent individual; he refused to cut down the food. He said, " I cannot feed the men on less than I am using now. I am careful, but I turn back cheap food, poor or tainted meat and poor vegetables that come to the camp. I cannot do better than I am doing." Well the superintendent, or whoever it was, said, "You will have to do better." The oook replied, " I cannot do it," and he threw off his apron and said, " Get somebody else." Somebody else took over the job, but evidently whatever this man was he was not a cook. After he had been there a few days the men found that there was less sugar on the table than had been usual. After a few more days the sugar disappeared altogether. Then a little later the dried fruits disappeared also, and the men were wondering what was wrong. For a time the flunkies who cleaned up the camp at night were given tea and toast after they had cleaned out the buildings, but this also was discontinued; they were turned out as soon as their work was finished and the doors of the cookhouse were locked. The men knew there was something wrong and they began to make investigations of their own. One of the men came into the camp one morning and said, " I have found it, boys. They have a still here; they are making home brew. That is where our prunes, our figs and our sugar have been going." The home brew was being made in the fire buckets.

Did the men get their
share of it?

No, it was all saved for
the higher ups. The men went to the foreman of the camp; they showed him the mash and said, "What are you going to do about it?" "Well," he said, "we will have to call in the provincial police." They called in the provincial police and showed them this mash; the police took the pails and dumped it out. The men said, "What are you going to do? Are you not going to prosecute somebody?" The police replied, "Well, there is no evidence." This may or may not be true, but that statement was made before the council and mayor of the city of Vancouver; in my opinion it should have been investigated but there has been no investigation. After considerable negotiation better counsel prevailed; the authorities did not accept the dictum of the Prime Minister that nothing should be done. On the promise that an effort would be made to get an investigation into their complaints, the men went back to camp quietly.
On Friday of last week I w'as in the city of Kingston, where I addressed a meeting which was attended by quite a number of men from one of the relief camps, and as usual these men had a number of complaints. The hon. member for New Westminster referred to the potatoes in one of the British Columbia camps. If my information is correct British Columbia camps are not the only ones where they have poor potatoes. The man who spoke to me said you could take the potatoes that were put on the table at that camp and if you squeezed them they would squirt water like a syringe. He also said that you could scrape the mould off the meat with a knife. In my opinion these are statements that the government Cannot afford to have broadcast without investigation. A young fellow from a camp near Toronto told me they were fed sour potatoes in that camp. He complained to the person in charge, and that person told him he was an agitator and that if there was any more of it he would have to get out. As soon as a man makes a complaint in a camp he is an agitator. In my opinion the people of this country ought to thank God that these men have enough manhood to complain, and I think we ought to take some notice of their complaints. The men themselves admit, of course, that there are agitators in the camps, but they say that every man who makes a complaint is not an agitator. They say that the camps are not the place for the men who are habitual
Supply-National Defence

agitators. Possibly the men are sick, either mentally or physically, and should not be in the camps. I suppose those camps cannot be abolished immediately, but surely we are not going to have them from now on. Young men reaching the age of twenty-one years are entering the camps, and old men are dropping out. Any government which does not clean up this situation has failed, I do not care what else it has done, and I would say that the sooner the government gets busy and tries to do something the better it will be for the Dominion of Canada.

I have another point
in mind, and it has to do with men who suffer accidents while in relief camps. In Ontario there is a workmen's compensation board, but men in camps who suffer accidents do not come within the jurisdiction of that board. Injuries suffered by civilians in the employ of the federal government are dealt with under legislation for government employees' compensation, and the government should consider action which would protect men who are injured in unemployment camps. I have in mind a young man who lost four fingers while operating a circular saw. I need not tell the government about the serious disability under which that young man will have to labour for the rest of his life. Under present regulations the person in question cannot be compensated, because he is working in the camp at Kingston which has in hand a project in connection with a college. Could the minister tell us whether this matter of compensation is being investigated? The family of the boy have seen me, because naturally they have had some cause for worry. Undoubtedly in after life due to the loss of his fingers he will be working under a disadvantage, and because of that handicap I - believe the government should make some provision for him. Certainly something should be done in the province in which they have the best workmen's compensation legislation in the world. Could the minister give hon. members some assurance that machinery will be set in motion whereby these young men who have suffered accidents and are unable to follow their normal work will receive compensation equal to what they would have received had they been in private industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Let me hasten to assure the hon. member for East Hamilton that the matter to which he has referred is being considered, and an arrangement has been arrived at between the departments of justice, labour and national defence with regard to the
LMr. Maclnnis.]
adjudication which shall be given in cases of accidents within camps. Probably the settlement will be along the lines of compensation offered under workmen's compensation legislation in the provinces. I need hardly say that the statements made by the hon. members for New Westminster, Vancouver North and Vancouver South will be most carefully investigated. Some of the representations the department has already heard; some have already been investigated, and no evidence has been found to justify them.
The committee will recall that the Department of National Defence comes into the picture because it has certain officials scattered throughout the dominion capable of taking over the work of overseeing camps. The provincial government approached the federa. government requesting assistance in the handling of the relief problem, and' as a result of agreements with each of the provinces the dominion government made it its business to look after the single homeless unemployed men. These men were placed in existing camps taken over from the provinces or in new camps built by the Department of National Defence. The men were given sustenance, fuel, shelter, and an allowance of tobacco in weight but not in price, as the hon. member has said. Work was provided for them under conditions which were considered reasonable. I have had many opportunities to visit the camps in southern British Columbia. I visited them during the last summer and fall, and the summer and fall prior to that. I have taken meals in them and have talked with the men; I have observed the work they were doing and have come to the conclusion that the camps-every one of them-bore a favourable relation to the camps in which I myself had worked in earlier years. The food was excellent, the conditions for sleeping were excellent, recreation facilities were good, and for men who unfortunately for the time were unable to find gainful occupation I would say they lived under reasonably happy surroundings. We must remember the dominion government comes into the matter simply to assist the provinces. Our work is one of assistance, not one of substitution of the task devolving upon the provincial governments.
The hon. member for New Westminster has raised the difficult problem of supplying the camps with the various kinds of foods. Obviously from the point of view of the taxpayer it is desirable and necessary that costs of camps be kept down to a reasonable minimum. When the average for all camps throughout Canada is struck it will be found that they are being run at an extremely low figure, and yet the balanced ration offered in

Supply-National Defence
each camp from the Atlantic to the Pacific is such that I personally could not complain. In my visits to the camps of which no notice had been given, I was handed meals which were most satisfactory in quantity and excellent in quality. I believe that from the point of view of food the men in the camps have very little to grumble about. The question of supplies by contract is one which offers some difficulty. There is no doubt whatever that the farmers in my constituency would like to be in a position to supply more beef, vegetables and other requirements than so far they have been allowed to supply, due to the system of contracting. Speaking more particularly about beef may I say that hon. members will undoubtedly realize the difficulty with which superintendents are faced when they attempt to arrange the supply of beef, especially in hot weather. Suppose we have a camp of one hundred men which requires a certain quantity of beef so many times a week. Farmers in the neighbourhood may have beasts to kill, but it does not follow that they are in a position definitely to guarantee that on a certain Wednesday they will be able to supply the camp with so many pounds of fresh beef. On the other hand, where you have firms who buy from the farmers, they have their own refrigerator arrangements and can definitely undertake to supply on such and such a day of the week so many pounds of beef for that camp. That is a means of getting over the difficulty which exists in endeavouring to buy comparatively small quantites of beef on certain days of the week.
The hon. member for Vancouver South has raised the question of the difficulties which occurred in the British Columbia camps in December. I think perhaps that situation has been adequately ventilated. The main point he makes is that investigation by a committee has so far been refused. The reason for that refusal is this: At any camp in Canada it is possible for a man having an objection to lay that objection before the foreman. If he is not satisfied with the reception he gets from the foreman he can take it to the superintendent of that group of camps.
The evidence is very much the other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If he is not satisfied with the reception he receives from the superintendent he can take it to the officer of that district. In the case of British Columbia, however, remembering that the dominion government is in this picture to help the province by agreement on terms laid down, the provincial government has been requested to send 92582-90
its representative into any or all of the camps and make up its own mind whether there is room for an investigation or not. So far as my knowledge goes, that investigation has not so far taken place. But the view taken by the department undoubtedly is that while we welcome visits of individuals, responsible men or ordinary citizens, we are not prepared to receive committees which will go in and investigate conditions and make their reports to we don't know whom.

The mere existence of these camps indicates a collapse in the system of which the members of this house should take cognizance. To say that in a system of society in which the potential productivity is almost beyond computation we have to shove men away in this sort of regimentation certainly does not imply any praise of the mentality of those who are the governing force in the country. It may be it is the only course they are able to follow at the present time ,and under the present system, but the time has surely come when in the light of conditions they must reconsider the whole position of camps of this kind and determine definitely whether or not they must accept as permanent a condition of unemployment involving the continuance of this sort of thing if the present system continues.
But I rose not to make any generalized statement on this question, as that can await a more appropriate moment, but rather to draw the minister's attention to some complaints that have come to me. While I cannot vouch for their accuracy I feel it incumbent on me to pass them on to the minister and to his department.
It is alleged that men are drifting into the cities from these camps as they are being ejected, devoid of means, poorly clad, and with no prospect of even obtaining a meal, refused by the dominion, provincial and civic authorities; and that at the moment of the writing of this document to me, namely, January 25 last, twenty-eight men are being fed in the city of Calgary from contributions gathered from relief recipients in the city itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Would my hon. friend say what camps they came from?

I can tell the minister one in any case before we get through. This is regarded as a callous attitude on the part of the authorities. Again I say the action may be justified. I leave it to the minister to investigate the facts.
With regard to camp No. 3, project 155, Seebe, it is alleged that one tent is supplied for ablutions in which 128 men take turns at

Supply-National Defence

two tubs for all purposes, washing, bathing and washing of clothes. I took this matter up with the department in the form of a question. I find that this is their reply to that charge, and I would ask hon. members to note it carefully:
Accommodation is temporarily being provided by using two contractors' tents, one for ablution and the other for laundry purposes, containing ablution basins, twelve wash tubs, one hand washing machine and two vacuum washers. Regular ablution hut now erected and fittings being installed.
I have no doubt at all that that is being done now, but I would ask the minister to find out whether the complaint registered was accurate at any time. Evidently the conditions are being improved in that regard.
The second complaint is that the water supply at that point is a hole in the ground; that the water seeps through into this hole, apparently a dug well, and that the same water used for washing purposes is also used for culinary purposes. Perhaps that is put the wrong way round, and that what is meant is that the culinary water is used for washing purposes. The reply to that complaint which I received from the department was this:
At present water hauled from spring by team in forty-five gallon drums. Gravity system from spring one thousand feet away under construction.
I would like to know whether it is a spring that the water was being taken from, or is the complaint well founded that the water was taken from a hole in the ground?
The next complaint is that these men have been called out to work when the temperature has been as low as twenty below zero. I think the department admits when it replies that the men are sent out in such temperatures to cut firewood.
The fourth complaint is that in the bunk-houses, if the men hang up their clothes at night, they will sometimes be found frozen to the walls in the morning. The department admits that the inside walls of all huts were very cold during cold spells.
The next complaint is that men making complaints either for themselves or on behalf of others are immediately ejected from camp, and that their lives are placed in jeopardy by reason of the fact that certain of their camp clothes are taken from them and that they are transported in open trucks in subzero weather and dumped into the cities and summarily disposed of. They are placed on a blacklist and denied entrance to any other camp should they desire to go there. They are cut off entirely from relief and told to fend for themselves. Obviously, if this is

true it must undoubtedly be one of the causes of crime. The official statement of these men is that this has come to be an alarming situation and is growing to such proportions that we cannot cope with it. I received this communication from the United Workers' Council of Delegates, Calgary. They go on to request that I take the matter up with the department in the hope that some action will be taken in connection with these complaints. I hope the minister will look into that too.

I desire to substantiate from personal knowledge all the remarks that have been made by my friends from British Columbia, the hon. members for New Westminster, Vancouver North, and Vancouver South. During the Christmas season we spent three whole days in the city of Vancouver and met a delegation from these men in the camps. Twelve hundred in round numbers came to the city of Vancouver, and I was greatly impressed by the exceeding fairness of the three spokesmen of these men who appeared before us. There was a complete lack of extremism, a complete absence of exaggeration in their statements, and a reasonable plea for fair play from the authorities.
The minister was exceedingly fair in his presentation of the case this evening, and I assure him at once that I am not going to impute the slightest blame to him because he has not been very long in charge of the department. But I suggest to him that he can do a tremendous amount to humanize the national defence camps in Canada. I am speaking with particular reference to British Columbia. What the hon. member for New Westminster said in regard to supplies is abundantly true, especially in the Kamloops area, where supplies have been bought from favoured contractors at prices higher than are charged by local farmers, and that in numerous instances. That is wrong, as I think the minister will agree. He mentioned the question of an investigation. Now, we promised these men in Vancouver that there would be an investigation, and after all, when three men are speaking for a number of men as in this instance, and when they ask for an impartial investigation, there is nothing unfair about such a request. The minister said that the provincial government had been asked to investigate; he is correct. And he is also right in saying that they refused to investigate and, I think, correctly so, because the provincial government has no jurisdiction whatever in regard to this method of handling relief. This is completely a national method, the only one that is completely national. We

Supply-National Defence
promised these men in all sincerity that there would be an impartial investigation. A committee from the council of social agencies in Vaueouver approached us, and I would ask the minister to appoint his own commission, one single commissioner in his own department, to investigate the complaints. I am satisfied, after listening to the representations that have been made, that he would find the complaints fully justified. I am sure that the minister, who is an exceedingly fair minded and humanitarian gentleman, will be the first to see that these practices which the men complain of will be remedied. He said that those men who were blacklisted and fired could go to the foreman, the superintendent or the local officer. Well, they were fired inside of five seconds without seeing the foreman; they were fired by the straw bosses in the camps without a moment's notice, without packing their clothing or having an item of food, and they were sent away to live or die. That was done, not by my hon. friend but under the jurisdiction and control of the department over which he now presides, and every word said by the bon. member for Vancouver South is abundantly justified by the evidence we heard. I appeal to the minister to appoint his own commissioner and send him to British Columbia, and I am sure that he would find justification for these boys' grievances.

May I point out to the minister, in connection with the purchase of supplies, that when the provincial government handled these camps the cost of meals-and I saw the figures before I left-ran from twenty-four to twenty-six cents per day for three meals for a man, averaging roughly eight cents per meal. Now the meals provided for the men in the camps under the jurisdiction of the provincial government were as good as if not more ample than the meals now provided by the dominion government. Before this item goes through I think we should have a statement from the minister as to the total cost of the men in the oamps, segregating meals from clothing and other supplies as well as tobacco. I say this because I take a great deal of pride in the accuracy of any statements I make to this house, and the statements I have made this evening are not hearsay; they are based on first hand information from the records of the camp itself-not what someone in the camp told me. I have seen the men supplied with meals both under the dominion and under the provincial jurisdiction, and I know that the province had no difficulty in getting meat. In regard to keeping meat fresh, so far as the camps in White Rock are concerned, there is
92582-90J
no difficulty because they have a freezing plant of their own, and the animals can be killed and the meat hung up and kept indefinitely. So that the question of keeping supplies fresh does not enter into the matter at all. When the provincial government was buying supplies locally there might be individual complaints, but apart from that the farmers supplied the rations such as fresh milk, vegetables, potatoes, pork, meat and other necessities, at reasonable rates, and I maintain that the price was a little less than the dominion government is now paying for the men in the camps. I submit that we should have a detailed statement of the whole cost, segregating clothing from the food supplied the men; and we might have the figures for the various provinces so that we might make a comparison.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Certainly the matter to
which the hon. member for Bow River drew attention will be investigated. It was the subject matter of a question which he placed on the order paper some weeks ago and which was answered. It will be gone into more fully, he having drawn it to the attention of the committee. He mentioned one point with regard to water being obtained from a hole in the ground. Water frequently is obtained from a hole in the ground, and when we are discussing the relief camps it should not be forgotten that there is a medical officer, one of whose duties is to keep his eye on the purity of the water required in the camp. I remember one of the camps not very far from where I live-fifty miles north of where I live-on the borders of a lake. It did not draw its water from that lake, and of course there was local gossip immediately to the effect, "Here is the dominion government laying two thousand feet of pipe down the hillside when it could have taken water from the lake." The reason the water was not taken from the lake was that there was a medical officer attached to the camp. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre raises the point once more of an investigation, and he states, as his reason for emphasizing the request for an investigation from Ottawa, that the responsibility is that of the dominion government. Now that is precisely where I differ from my hon. friend; the responsibility is that of the provincial government; the dominion government comes into the picture, let me repeat, in aid of but not in substitution for the work done by the provincial government. My hon. friend from New Westminster has raised the question of costs, and I think he
Supply-National Defence

said, if I understood him rightly, that the ration cost to the government was 24 cents a day.
From 24 to 26.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps I might read to the committee, in order to put it on the record, the expenditure per man day on relief to September 30 last. This totals $1.30 per man day and includes, so far as I am aware, everything that can properly be charged to the relief camp.

That is roughly $31 per man;
$1.30 per day would be roughly $31.

as anybody over there.

from the looks of you.

I have listened to remarks the most exaggerated and unfair and what I consider-
Order.

From my own personal
knowledge I can say that I have never listened to a more exaggerated statement made in this house than the hon. gentleman has made to-night, nor than another statement the hon. member made in regard to the empire agreements, altogether erroneous statements. Again to-night he is repeating the same thing.
While I am on my feet may I have this opportunity of saying something in regard to the statements made by the hon. member for Bow River. The statements were made in the press before the city council of Calgary, and the medical health officer of that city accompanied by two other representative citizens, one the president of the unemployed associations of that city and the other an alderman, went out to investigate the charges which were made. Not the statements which the hon. member has made to-night, but those which appeared in the press, the reported gist of which the hon. member has repeated to-night, were investigated, and the medical health officer reported to the city council that the statements were altogether exaggerated; that the camps after a most thorough and careful examination were found to be healthy, the food was found to be splendid; the sanitary conditions were found to be excellent and the camps were quite desirable. He

pointed out several drawbacks because of the transition period through which they were passing in establishing the new camps, but otherwise the camps were quite desirable.

The hon. member for East Calgary will do me the justice of remembering that I made no statements. I quoted, as I carefully pointed out to the minister, remarks for which I did not accept responsibility and merely asked that they be investigated.

I endeavoured to make it appear in that way in my remarks. The gist of the inquiries which the hon. member made was taken from reports in the press and investigated by this special committee of which I have spoken.

I take the strongest exception to the remarks of the hon. member for East Calgary. I can tell him that many members may make statements in the house, but the statements I have made this evening I can challenge any hon. member, even the minister, to dispute. They were given to me right from the camp. It may well be the remarks I made regarding the medical profession are pinching my hon. friend a little hard. The statement with regard to the Ottawa agreements I will deal with at some other time, but so far they have not been controverted. It is true one member attempted to controvert them and said that I had made a mistake in regard to the question of butter, but it did not affect my argument at all. But the statements I made regarding the economic conference agreements were made from the government record, and as to the statements I made with regard to the camps, I will put my seat in jeopardy along with his if he cares to dispute them. I got my facts directly from the camp. I was told by the man in charge that the price paid for potatoes was $24 a ton, wdiile as I have stated the farmer was getting $5 a ton for grade number one and $3.75 for grade number two. Will he undertake now to say that my statements are wrong?
When I mentioned the price of tobacco the minister took me to task and said that tobacco was provided. Perhaps 1.3 cents is all that is allowed each man, and it may not be allowed in cash, but those statements were taken down by me just a few days before I left for Ottawa and I repeat that they were given to me by the man in charge of the camp, an appointee of the government.

The minister stated a few minutes ago that the care of the single homeless men was very largely a provincial and not a federal responsibility; that therefore any investigation into conditions prevailing in those camps in British Columbia and in other provinces could very well be conducted by the provincial authorities and that the assistance rendered by the minister's department was not in substitution but in aid of provincial relief. I wish to take the most strenuous objection to that statement, because I saw that stated in several telegrams which passed between the
Prime Minister and some of us in Vancouver during the negotiations to which I referred previously. Rightly or wrongly the Department of National Defence and the federal government have assumed in those camps the sole and entire responsibility for the care of those single homeless men. When accusations are made, rightly or wrongly, in regard to malpractices in those camps I suggest to the minister that his immediate duty is not to ask any provincial government to investigate them but to send his own commissioners out to those camps in British Columbia and other provinces and to assume the complete burden of investigation. I am certain, if the minister does that, it will assist him in the future administration of this very difficult problem. The minister and the government are wrong in trying to shelve their obvious responsibilty in regard to those camps. Rightly or wrongly the Department of National Defence assumed complete control over those men and to-day they are charged with entire responsibility for their care. To try to shift the responsibility to the provincial government is an evasion of the responsibility this government must assume and maintain in days to come. I am asking the minister in his own interest to investigate conditions in those camps and I am certain this will help him and his department in the administration of the whole system in future days.
Progress reported.
